assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 60,000 req/s peak. 80% are online feature lookups on the inference path, 19.4% raw feature events arriving on the bus, 0.5% training-set reads, 0.1% (60/s) batch backfill partitions.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: 92% of online lookups are served from the Redis feature store; the 8% miss falls through to the point-in-time store (db visit_prob 0.08). Feature vectors are large values, so a node is modelled at 50k ops/s rather than the 100k a counter workload would give.

assumptions.subject: stream
assumptions.statement: The transformer writes a materialised feature for roughly half the events it sees (cache visit_prob 0.5) — the rest are inputs to a window that has not closed yet. Training/serving skew and point-in-time correctness are CORRECTNESS properties this engine does not model at all; it sizes the pipeline, it does not validate the features.

assumptions.subject: batch
assumptions.statement: A backfill task is one partition of a training set, ~500 ms of work, so an instance sustains ~2 tasks/s. The fleet is sized for a steady 60 partitions/s. A real backfill is bursty — this is the smoothed average, and the engine has no way to express the burst.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: Compute only. Lake storage (GB-month), object-store requests and GPU inference are outside this model — inference itself is a separate service that CALLS this pipeline.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: Kafka broker capacity is modelled at 200,000 messages/s per broker (3 brokers). Source: Confluent's benchmark (confluent.io/blog/kafka-fastest-messaging-system/, published 2020-08-21) measured 605 MB/s of peak stable throughput across 3 i3en.2xlarge brokers at 1 KB messages with replication factor 3 — about 200k msg/s per broker. LinkedIn's 2014 run (engineering.linkedin.com, '2,024,032 records/sec' across three machines, 100-byte messages, 3x ASYNCHRONOUS replication) implies roughly 675k/broker; the lower, larger-message, synchronous-RF=3 Confluent figure is the one used here. The value this replaces — 5,000 msg/s per broker — sat 40x to 135x below both published figures, which made the event bus look like the thing to buy more of. It is not: at a cited broker rate the bus is close to idle and the binding constraint is the streaming transformer, which is where a real feature pipeline is sized.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: MISMATCH, declared rather than hidden: the broker THROUGHPUT above was measured on i3en.2xlarge hardware, while this row's PRICE is the AWS MSK kafka.t3.small broker-hour rate. Those are not the same machine — a t3.small broker will not sustain 200k msg/s. This model has no way to tie a capacity citation to a price citation, so read the bus cost line as a placeholder for 'three brokers', not as the cost of the hardware the benchmark ran on. Sizing a real cluster means pricing the broker class you actually benchmark.

assumptions.subject: stream
assumptions.statement: With the bus corrected, 2,500 events/s per transformer instance becomes the load-bearing number in this design — it alone decides which component binds and where the design breaks — and it has NO published source. It is an author's engineering estimate for a stateful windowed transform on one m6i.large. Real per-operator throughput in Flink or Spark Structured Streaming swings by an order of magnitude with window size, state backend, serialisation format and key skew, so this figure should be replaced by a measurement of your own job before any fleet is sized from it.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The 8% fall-through from the online store to the point-in-time store (db visit_prob 0.08) is a modelling simplification that is kept here, with its limits stated. Feast's documentation (docs.feast.dev/getting-started/components/offline-store) gives the offline store two purposes — 'Building training datasets from time-series features' and 'Materializing (loading) features into an online store to serve those features at low-latency in a production setting' — and the online-store page states that 'for each entity key, only the latest feature values are stored. No historical values are stored.' Neither page says what happens on a miss, so this blueprint does NOT claim that Feast returns null. What it does flag is this: in a materialised feature store the real failure mode of an online-store miss is usually a degraded or missing feature vector — a CORRECTNESS incident that skews inference — rather than the extra database load this edge models. The engine sizes load; it cannot see that failure. Dropping the edge would lower db's computed arrivals but would not change which component binds.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Open storage-layout question this model does not resolve: is one online lookup ONE Redis operation on a serialized feature vector (fan-out 1, which is what is modelled here), or one operation PER FEATURE (a fan-out of 50-250)? Hopsworks' vendor benchmark (2023-12-22, measuring itself against Feast) 'gradually increased the number of features in the vector from 50 to 250', but it is a P99 LATENCY test at a constant 10 RPS and does not establish operations per feature. The 50k ops/s per-node derate used here — supported by redis.io's benchmark note that 'processing 10 bytes, 100 bytes, or 1000 bytes queries almost result in the same throughput' against a measured 'SET: 180180.17 requests per second' unpipelined on a 3-byte payload — covers only the serialized-vector layout. Under a field-per-feature layout the cache's arrivals would be multiplied by the feature count and this sizing would not hold.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: The 80% online-lookup / 19.4% event-ingest split is an author's estimate, not a measured ratio. It is write-heavy for a feature store, and no primary source establishing the true read:write ratio of a production feature store was found — saying so is more honest than citing one that does not exist. This matters because the ingest share alone sets the load on the bus and the transformer, and the transformer is the component this design names as its constraint: a different split moves the constraint.

_library.summary: Feature store with a Redis online-serving tier, a streaming materialiser off an event bus, and batch backfill from the offline lake.
